title: GPU runtime profiling: TensorRT-LLM/vLLM/CUDA graphs - deep dive with Orion Tech
summary: Deep technical session focused on GPU runtime profiling: kernel selection, TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM tradeoffs, CUDA graph benefits, batching and KV cache behavior, and quantization impacts. Agreed to run a joint benchmark on Orion sample workload (chat + long context) in a VPC pilot; Redwood to share benchmark spreadsheet, kernel traces, and suggested quantization profiles.
next_steps: Maya to send benchmark spreadsheet and slide deck (includes kernel selection notes) - by 2026-03-13
Orion to share representative prompt set and 1M-token sample trace - by 2026-03-18
Schedule pilot kickoff (30d) once initial benchmarks are run - tentative week of 3/23
action_items: Liam: export CUDA graph traces and kernel-level logs for the two model variants - 2026-03-14
Rina: provide sample prompts, typical seq lengths, and token distribution - 2026-03-18
Tom: confirm VPC networking and GPU instance types for pilot (will consider A100x2 vs H100x1) - 2026-03-16
transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:05] Daniel (Orion CTO): Daniel here.
[00:07] Rina (Orion ML): Rina on the line.
[00:09] Tom (Orion Infra): Tom joining.
[00:11] Liam (Redwood SE): Liam from Redwood.
[00:13] Maya: Great — objective for today is a deep dive into GPU runtime profiling. We want to compare TensorRT-LLM and vLLM behavior, look at kernel selection, CUDA graphs, KV cache impacts, batching, and quantization tradeoffs, especially in VPC/on-prem contexts.
[00:30] Daniel: Sounds good. Our main concerns are p99 latency for chat, cost per token, and ability to run a private VPC deployment with strict KMS policies.
[00:45] Rina: Also curious about long context behavior — we do a lot of 8k-32k sequences, and KV cache growth is our top perf pain.
[00:58] Liam: Totally. We'll surface traces that show KV cache memory pressure and how different runtimes manage KV eviction and continuous batching. Quick note: some of the automated transcripts swap words — forgive that.
[01:12] Maya: We'll kick off with kernel selection basics. Liam, want to take that?
[01:16] Liam: Sure. So, kernel selection is, uh, basically choosing the best CUDA/cuBLAS/cuDNN/TensorRT kernels for ops like attention, matmuls, and rotary embeddings. In practice, TensorRT-LLM tends to pick fused attention kernels optimized for the GPU compute capability, especially for H100 where TF32+tensor cores change the equation. vLLM (we'll call it vLLM for shorthand) uses more generic kernels but has very efficient KV cache packing and batching heuristics.
[01:45] Rina: Are you seeing major perf diffs for shorter sequences?
[01:49] Liam: For short seq (<=128) TensorRT-LLM often wins latency — lower per-token p50. For longer seq (>2k) the kernel scheduling and memory strategy matter more; vLLM sometimes has better throughput because of its continuous batching and lighter-weight kernel overheads. But when you enable TensorRT cuDNN fused kernels and use CUDA graphs, the gap narrows.
[02:20] Tom: Can you explain the CUDA graph bit? We haven't used graphs in production.
[02:25] Liam: Yeah, CUDA graphs let you record a sequence of GPU ops once and replay them, avoiding launch overhead. For autoregressive generation with consistent shapes and batching patterns, graphs can reduce CPU-GPU sync and boost qps and reduce tail latency. The caveat: graphs are shape-sensitive — if your batch sizes or sequence lengths change, you need multiple graphs or fall back.
[02:47] Daniel: So for our mixed load (small chat requests + occasional long summarization jobs) how do we use graphs?
[02:53] Liam: Common approach is to have a small set of graphs: e.g., graph for seq<128 batch 1..8, graph for seq 512 batch up to 4, and a fallback path. Redwood's runtime can auto-select the best graph and fall back to JIT kernels if shape mismatch occurs. There's overhead for maintaining multiple graphs and memory for their scratch buffers.
[03:18] Rina: What about KV cache memory — we saw OOMs when session lengths hit 20k tokens. Do kernels differ here?
[03:25] Liam: Not so much the kernel, it's more KV layout and memory allocation strategy. vLLM tends to use a packed KV format with 1D contiguous buffers facilitating prefetching. TensorRT-LLM may keep per-layer KV in separate buffers which can cause fragmentation but allows layer-wise swap-out. For very long contexts, quantized KV and offloading (CPU or NVMe) come into play.
[03:50] Maya: Quick interruption — we have a slide deck and benchmark spreadsheet we'll share after the call (link in notes). Liam, can you walk through a recent benchmark?
[03:58] Liam: Yeah. So we ran a 13B chat model on H100x1 and A100x2. Baseline: vLLM with dynamic batching, no CUDA graphs, FP16 weights. TensorRT-LLM used TRT fused kernels, CUDA graphs for stable shapes, and QAT/INT8 for some layers. Results: p50 latency for single-token generation — TensorRT-LLM ~12ms, vLLM ~18ms. Throughput at saturation (multi-concurrent sessions generating) — vLLM and TRT similar when batch sizes grow because vLLM's batching is very effective. But cost per token varied: TRT+INT8 reduced GPU utilization time per token ~25% lower.
[04:46] Daniel: Is that with KV cache enabled?
[04:49] Liam: Yes KV cache on both. The trick was memory layout: TRT implementation reduced memory copies during KV updates, which helped for shorter latencies. For very long sessions, the per-token compute is lower but memory bandwidth dominates, so quantization and kernel memory access patterns matter most.
[05:10] Rina: About quantization — we saw hallucination spikes when we applied heavy quantization. What's safe?
[05:16] Liam: Right. INT8 across the whole model can affect generation quality; recommended approach is mixed quantization: activations and most matmuls in FP16, only attention MG or linear layers can be INT8 with calibration. Redwood Optimize can suggest layer-wise quant profiles and run evals against your prompt sets to measure quality regressions.
[05:37] Tom: For VPC/on-prem, how does NVIDIA driver/KMS interplay? We need HSM and customer-managed KMS; can Redwood still run TRT optimizations?
[05:47] Maya: Yes — on Private deployments we ship a control plane but the model artifacts and keys stay in your VPC. For on-prem air-gapped, we have an install bundle. TensorRT and CUDA are in the environment; you manage the drivers. Redwood can provide guidance for driver versions we validated.
[06:06] Daniel: Networking and kernel licensing — any special permissions?
[06:10] Liam: Just Nvidia driver licensing plus typical CUDA toolkit. For Triton it's similar. Nothing unusual from Redwood's side, but we'll give a compatibility matrix in the doc.
[06:20] Maya: Let's look at a quick trace. Liam, pull up the kernel timeline.
[06:25] Liam: (screen share) Okay, here's a kernel flame for an attention pass. You can see fused attention kernel A dominating, then cuBLASGemm for FFN; on H100 the attention kernel has much lower execution time thanks to warp-level intrinsics. Note the tiny spikes where KV copy happens — that's where tail latency jumps.
[06:47] Rina: Those KV spikes — are they synchronous CPU->GPU memcpy?
[06:51] Liam: Sometimes yes, especially if the runtime lazily allocates. Redwood's runtime tries to pre-allocate large resident KV buffers and use asynchronous memcpy with CUDA streams, but if memory is fragmented or graphs force a synchronous path, you see those spikes.
[07:06] Tom: How do graphs interact with async memcpy?
[07:09] Liam: You can record memcpy operations into graphs, but pinned allocations are required; recorded graphs assume the buffers exist at record time. If you dynamically reallocate, you break the graph. So for graphs you need stable buffers — which pushes you to pre-allocate KV capacity or use slab allocators.
[07:26] Daniel: So tradeoff: lower tail latency using graphs vs flexibility for variable seq lengths.
[07:31] Liam: Exactly. For Orion, if your usage pattern is 70% short chat and 30% long jobs, a hybrid approach is recommended — graphs for the frequent short paths, fallback JIT for the rest.
[07:47] Rina: About batching — what's Redwood's strategy to balance latency and cost?
[07:51] Liam: We do adaptive batching: small requests are grouped for a short timer window (e.g., 5-10ms) to boost GPU throughput without increasing p99 beyond SLO. For enterprise you can pin dedicated instances with predictable throughput. Also we have priority routing to let high-tier customers skip batching if latency-critical.
[08:10] Daniel: We might need dedicated for compliance and guaranteed throughput. What's the typical commit size?
[08:14] Maya: Dedicated contracts vary; we can propose options. For pilot we'd start hosted or a small private VPC reserve.
[08:21] Tom: Another infra detail — what about NUMA and multi-GPU kernel placement for A100x2? Does kernel selection consider peer-to-peer NVLink transfer costs?
[08:30] Liam: Yes, kernel scheduler prefers colocated kernels to reduce NVLink hops. For multi-GPU we use model parallel slicing where possible, but for 13B models it's often better to keep to single GPU where possible. A100x2 benefits from large batch workloads where we shard batches across GPUs and overlap compute and memcpy.
[08:51] Rina: Any differences in latency determinism between H100 and A100?
[08:55] Liam: H100 with its DPX/Tensor core improvements tends to be faster but can have less deterministic perf if mixed precision heuristics change. A100 is a bit more predictable in our tests; H100 needs tuned kernel selection and driver versions. We'll include versioned perf numbers.
[09:12] Maya: We're getting a few questions in chat — one asks about Triton vs Redwood runtime.
[09:17] Liam: Quick take: Triton is a great orchestration layer; Redwood runtime focused on continuous batching, KV-aware optimizations, and model-aware kernel selection. We can interop with Triton as well.
[09:29] Daniel: Ok can we talk about measurement methodology? When you report p50/p95/p99, how are you getting those?
[09:36] Liam: We run representative request traces replayed through a load generator that replays arrival times and payload sizes. We capture GPU timelines (ns resolution), kernel times, memcpy times, and NVLink events. We measure cold vs warm (cold meaning no cached graphs/no preallocated KV) and steady-state. We also run quality evals on a labeled prompt set to detect regressions from quantization.
[10:00] Rina: For our workloads the hot vs cold ratio is important because many sessions are long-lived; p99 during initial warmup spikes are ok but we care about steady-state.
[10:10] Liam: Good note — graphs aim to reduce steady-state p99. For warmup we do prewarming strategies.
[10:18] Maya: Let's jump to concrete pilot next steps. We proposed Redwood runs a 5-day benchmark using Orion sample traces on H100x1 and A100x2. We'll provide the scripts and ask Orion to validate results.
[10:34] Daniel: Fine. What artifacts do you need from us?
[10:38] Maya: Sample prompt set, token distribution, preferred model variant, and a network/VPC access window if we need to run in your VPC for private tests.
[10:46] Rina: We can share a sanitized prompt set and a 1M-token sample trace.
[10:50] Tom: I'll confirm GPU instance types we can provision and network windows.
[10:54] Liam: I'll add one more technical detail — kernel autotuner. Redwood runtime has an offline tuner that runs microbenchmarks across matmul shapes and picks best kernels; we persist a kernel selection table per GPU driver+CUDA version. That helps with H100 variance.
[11:12] Daniel: Any gotchas for ondemand scaling?
[11:15] Liam: When scaling out, you need to ensure graphs and cached KV are warmed on new instances; otherwise first requests to scaled nodes will be cold. We recommend a short warm-up burst and async preloading of KV for active sessions.
[11:29] Rina: Can Redwood expose token-level cost breakdowns during the pilot?
[11:33] Maya: Yes — Redwood Console will show token-level cost and latency breakdown per route/model. We'll share a sample dashboard.
[11:41] Daniel: Security checklist — SOC2, SSO, KMS, audit logs.
[11:44] Maya: We have SOC2 Type II, SAML/SSO, RBAC, and audit logs. For Private we can integrate with customer KMS/HSM. We'll drop security docs in the follow-up.
[11:55] Tom: For on-prem air-gap installs, how do software updates for TensorRT happen?
[11:59] Liam: We provide an install bundle and patch guidance; customers manage driver updates. For critical security patches Redwood provides guidance and offline artifacts as needed.
[12:08] Daniel: Anything else on kernels and CUDA graphs?
[12:11] Liam: Two practical tips: 1) Pre-allocate slab buffers for KV to make graphs viable and avoid fragment-induced syncs. 2) Use mixed graphs + JIT fallback to balance tail latency and flexibility.
[12:24] Rina: We should capture some real-world anomalies — we'll include a sample trace with those KV OOMs.
[12:29] Maya: Great. We'll run the bench, and then schedule a follow-up to review traces. Proposed time for pilot kickoff — week of 2026-03-23.
[12:39] Daniel: Works for us.
[12:41] Liam: I'll summarise the trace outputs we'll share: kernel timelines, CUDA graph recordings, KV buffer allocations, and the tuner output.
[12:50] Maya: Wrapping up — recap of next steps and owners in the chat. Thanks everyone.
[12:56] Rina: Thanks, this was useful.
[12:58] Daniel: Appreciate it.
[13:00] Tom: Thanks.
[13:02] Maya: End.

Notes: shared artifacts referenced — https://redwood.ai/decks/gpu-runtime-profiling.pdf (deck), https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/orion-sample-benchmarks.xlsx (benchmark spreadsheet). Some transcript words may be slightly off (e.g., "KV cash" in autosub).
